title: Unidirectional flow in a diode and an LED, and testing working order
shortTitle: Testing a diode with a multimeter
objective: To show with a multimeter that a diode and an LED conduct in one direction only.
To read the forward voltage drop and use it to identify the material of the junction.
To judge whether a given component is working, open or short-circuited.

theory.statement: A p-n junction conducts when it is forward-biased and blocks when it is reverse-biased. A multimeter on its diode range drives a small current through the junction and displays the forward voltage drop, which is about 0.7 V for silicon and about 1.8 to 2.0 V for a light-emitting diode. A healthy junction therefore shows a reading one way and an open-circuit indication the other. There are only two ways it can fail, and they are opposites: an OPEN junction conducts in neither direction, and a SHORTED junction conducts in both, with almost no voltage drop.
keyEquations: Forward bias conducts, reverse bias blocks: this is rectification.
The forward drop is a property of the material, so it identifies the junction.
An open fault gives no conduction either way.
A short fault gives conduction both ways at nearly zero ohms.
A verdict needs both directions; one reading can never establish a fault.

apparatus.name: Digital multimeter with a diode range
apparatus.why: The diode range supplies enough voltage to forward-bias an LED and reads the forward drop directly.

apparatus.name: Silicon diodes, good and faulty
apparatus.why: To establish the healthy pattern and then to recognise departures from it.

apparatus.name: LEDs, good and faulty
apparatus.why: To show that a light-emitting junction has a larger forward drop.

apparatus.name: Test leads with fine probes
apparatus.why: Component legs are close together; blunt probes short them.

procedure: Set the meter to its diode-test range.
Connect a known-good diode with its anode to the positive probe and read the display.
Reverse it and read again. Note that it conducts one way only.
Repeat with a good LED and compare the forward drops.
Now take each remaining component and test it in both directions.
Decide whether it is working, open or shorted, and record the verdict with both readings.

steps: For each component, compare the forward and reverse readings.
Reading one way, open the other → the junction is healthy.
Open both ways → the junction is open-circuit.
Conducting both ways at a very low value → the junction is shorted.

expectedResult.statement: A healthy diode reads about 0.7 V forward and open reverse; a healthy LED reads about 1.8 to 2.0 V forward and open reverse. Both therefore show unidirectional flow. A faulty component departs from this in one of exactly two ways: open in both directions, or conducting in both directions at nearly zero volts. Recognising which of the two has occurred is the object of the second half of the activity.

safety: Test components out of circuit. In circuit, a parallel path can make a good component look shorted.
Never use the diode range on a live circuit; the meter supplies its own voltage and the reading is meaningless.
Do not exceed the current rating of an LED when testing it outside the meter.
sourcesOfError: Testing in one direction only, which cannot establish either one-way flow or a fault.
Using the ohms range on an LED, where the meter may not supply enough voltage to make it conduct.
Testing in circuit, where a parallel component provides another path.
Confusing an open junction with a capacitor, since both read open.
Holding both probes and the component legs, so body resistance shunts the reading.

viva.question: What does unidirectional flow mean for a diode?
viva.expectedConcept: It conducts when forward-biased and blocks when reverse-biased.
viva.answerLogic: It conducts when forward-biased and blocks when reverse-biased.
viva.commonMisconception: That a diode resists current in one direction but still passes some.

viva.question: Why does the diode range show a voltage rather than a resistance?
viva.expectedConcept: The forward drop is a property of the junction, whereas an apparent resistance depends on the meter.
viva.answerLogic: The forward drop is a property of the junction, whereas an apparent resistance depends on the meter.
viva.commonMisconception: That the two ranges give equivalent information.

viva.question: A component reads 0.002 V forward and 0.002 V reverse. What is wrong?
viva.expectedConcept: The junction is shorted: it conducts both ways with no barrier, so it now behaves as a wire.
viva.answerLogic: The junction is shorted: it conducts both ways with no barrier, so it now behaves as a wire.
viva.commonMisconception: That a low reading always means good conduction and therefore a healthy component.

viva.question: A component reads OL in both directions. What are the possibilities?
viva.expectedConcept: An open junction, or a component that is not a junction at all, such as a capacitor.
viva.answerLogic: An open junction, or a component that is not a junction at all, such as a capacitor.
viva.commonMisconception: That OL always means the meter is on the wrong range.

viva.question: Why might a good LED fail to light on the ohms range?
viva.expectedConcept: The ohms range supplies too little current and often too little voltage to reach the forward drop.
viva.answerLogic: The ohms range supplies too little current and often too little voltage to reach the forward drop.
viva.commonMisconception: That a dark LED is a dead LED.

viva.question: How does the forward drop tell you the material?
viva.expectedConcept: Germanium is about 0.3 V, silicon about 0.7 V, a light-emitting junction 1.8 V or more.
viva.answerLogic: Germanium is about 0.3 V, silicon about 0.7 V, a light-emitting junction 1.8 V or more.

viva.question: Why must the component be out of circuit?
viva.expectedConcept: Parallel components offer other paths, so the meter measures the network rather than the diode.
viva.answerLogic: Parallel components offer other paths, so the meter measures the network rather than the diode.
viva.commonMisconception: That the meter isolates whatever its probes touch.

viva.question: What is the practical use of one-way conduction?
viva.expectedConcept: Rectification: converting alternating current to direct current.
viva.answerLogic: Rectification: converting alternating current to direct current.
viva.commonMisconception: That diodes are only protective devices.

viva.question: A student declares a diode faulty after one forward reading of OL. What is missing?
viva.expectedConcept: The reverse reading, and a check that the component was the right way round in the first place.
viva.answerLogic: The reverse reading, and a check that the component was the right way round in the first place.
viva.commonMisconception: That a single OL proves a fault.

viva.question: Why are open and short the only two failure modes considered here?
viva.expectedConcept: A junction either still blocks and conducts as designed, or it has broken open, or it has fused into a conductor.
viva.answerLogic: A junction either still blocks and conducts as designed, or it has broken open, or it has fused into a conductor.
viva.commonMisconception: That components fail in arbitrary partial ways that a meter cannot classify.

preLab.question: A healthy silicon diode on the diode range reads about:
preLab.feedback: Silicon junctions drop about 0.7 V; germanium about 0.3 V and an LED 1.8 V or more.

preLab.question: Reverse-biasing a healthy junction gives:
preLab.feedback: A healthy junction blocks in reverse, so the meter shows OL.

duringLab.question: Show one-way conduction on a known-good component first.
Test at least three different components and give a verdict on each.

postLab.question: The forward drop of an LED exceeds that of a silicon diode because:
postLab.feedback: The wider gap sets both the larger forward drop and the photon energy.

postLab.question: Testing a diode in circuit may mislead because:
postLab.feedback: In circuit the meter reads the network, not the diode alone.
